analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying generic rivals to keep cheaper copies off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past the Senate Judiciary Committee — one subcommittee hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015, despite a bipartisan slate of 7 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug maker challenges a brand-name drug's patent, the brand company can settle the lawsuit by paying the generic company to stay off the market for years — a practice known as 'pay for delay.' Consumers keep paying brand-name prices while the payment to the generic maker is typically far smaller than what the brand firm would lose to competition. This bill would let the Federal Trade Commission treat such settlements as presumptively unlawful, impose civil penalties of up to triple the value transferred, and require the companies' CEOs to certify under oath that they disclosed all related agreements, while leaving ordinary early-entry settlements alone.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need the drug, private health insurers, and taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid — all of whom keep paying brand-name prices for the months or years a pay-for-delay deal pushes a generic off the market. The bill's own findings note generics sometimes discount brand prices by more than 90 percent, and that generics are 67 percent of prescriptions but only 20 percent of drug spending [S3]. Anyone whose settlement gets blocked gets the generic sooner.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a legal presumption that a patent settlement is anticompetitive and unlawful when the generic filer receives anything of value and agrees to delay or limit its generic drug, with the burden on the companies to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the deal's pro-competitive benefits outweigh its harms [S2][S3].

Lets the FTC bring enforcement proceedings against the parties to such settlements and imposes civil penalties of up to three times the value received from the deal, and makes violating the section a violation of the FTC Act's ban on unfair methods of competition [S3].

Requires drug companies to file any side agreements made within 30 days of a settlement with the FTC and the Justice Department, and requires the CEO or the official who negotiated the deal to certify that the filing is complete and final — closing the door on undisclosed side deals [S2][S3].

Preserves legitimate settlements: the bill does not touch deals where the generic maker gets only early entry rights, reimbursement of litigation expenses up to $7.5 million, or a covenant not to sue — so settlements that genuinely bring a generic to market early stay legal [S3].

Strips a generic maker of its 180-day exclusivity period if a court or the FTC finds its settlement violated the act, so a company that cut an unlawful deal loses its head start rather than profiting from it [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose their ability to pay generic competitors to delay entry — deals the bill's findings describe as more profitable for both sides than competition [S3]. Generic manufacturers would lose the side payments they receive for staying off the market, though they would keep the main prize of selling generics. The $7.5 million cap on reimbursed litigation expenses could also make some legitimate settlements harder to reach.

drawbacks.text: The presumption of illegality combined with a 'clear and convincing evidence' burden — a very high legal standard — could deter even settlements that bring generics to market early, reducing the settlements the bill itself aims to encourage [S3].

The bill does not lower any drug's price directly and does not touch a brand company's patent rights; it only speeds competition where a delay was bought, so its benefits depend on how often pay-for-delay deals actually occur [S2][S3].

The $7.5 million cap on reimbursable litigation costs is modest for complex pharmaceutical patent litigation, which could push parties toward less transparent deal structures rather than fewer delay agreements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the trade is heavily favorable: the bill's own findings state that both the brand and generic makers profit from a delay deal relative to competition, and that consumers lose what the 1984 generic-approval law was meant to give them [S3]. The main cost — chilled settlements — is limited by the bill's explicit carve-outs for early-entry deals. The genuine weakness is enforcement design: a high evidentiary burden and a modest litigation-cost cap could push companies toward deals the law does not clearly catch, which is why the FTC also gets new reporting and certification powers under the bill [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held one subcommittee hearing in July 2013 but never took it up for a committee vote or sent it to the Senate floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on February 4, 2013, joined by original cosponsors including Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA), Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL), Sen. Al Franken (D-MN), and Sen. Tim Johnson (D-SD) [S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
The committee's Subcommittee on Antitrust, Competition Policy and Consumer Rights held a hearing on July 23, 2013 — the bill's only recorded action after referral [S5].
No further action was taken: the committee never marked up or voted on the bill, the Senate never debated it, and it expired with the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who kept using settlement payments to delay generic competition and extend monopoly-priced sales, and the generic manufacturers that received those payments. Patients, insurers, and taxpayers kept paying brand-name prices for the drugs whose cheaper copies were held off the market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and paid-off generic firms

against.role: Committee of jurisdiction under Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Referred to at introduction; held a single subcommittee hearing and never scheduled a markup or committee vote during the 113th Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers and the generic makers that accepted delay payments
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on reverse-payment settlements, which the industry has defended as legitimate patent litigation resolutions.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split across party lines — 5 Democrats, 1 Republican (Sen. Grassley of Iowa), and 1 Independent — but the bill never reached a vote, so no vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: These companies profit by settling patent challenges with payments that keep generics off the market, letting them sell at brand prices for months or years longer — deals the bill's findings call more profitable than competition [S3]. The bill would end that revenue stream; its defeat preserved it.

Generic makers receive 'anything of value' for agreeing to delay entry, which the bill would prohibit and penalize — but the same companies' core business, selling cheaper generics, gains whenever a delayed generic finally launches [S3]. Their interest in delay payments runs against patients; their interest in entering the market runs with them.

industries.industry: Health insurers and public programs (Medicare, Medicaid)
industries.note: These payers absorb drug costs and would benefit when generic competition arrives sooner; the bill's findings note federal dollars fund roughly 35 percent of national prescription drug spending [S3].
